image.caption: The furthest south, 9 January 1909
image.credit: From Shackleton's account of the expedition (1911) · public domain
image.why: The moment and the caption hold up. Shackleton's own book has a plate of the same three-men-and-Union-Jack scene captioned 'Farthest South, January 9, 1909', and his text has the flags hoisted at 88° 23′ that morning. The caption names nobody and doesn't say 'the party', so it's safe with four men south and one behind the camera. The public-domain reasoning doesn't hold as written. (1) The 1911 plate (PG 69138, img_pg_149, facing p. 149) is a different exposure from the Commons scan: the poses, mitts and flag-pole spacing differ. So 'published in 1909' is shown only for the moment, not for this photograph. (2) The photographer isn't settled. Commons lists Shackleton as 'Artist', but by AWI's own credit he stands in the frame. Secondary pages most often name Marshall (d. 1963), which would undo a 'died 70 years ago' basis, and unpublished US works run life + 70. (3) The UK line 'pre-1957 photograph, 70 years from publication' isn't the old-law rule (the 1911 Act counted from the negative). Fix: swap in Shackleton's published plate, which is public domain in the US by pre-1929 publication and carries his own caption and date (scan the 1909 *Heart of the Antarctic* plate if it's the same one, and credit that edition instead). Or keep this scan only once its pre-1929 publication or its photographer's term is shown.
